gancho: O veneno do baiacu, o fugu japonês, não é feito pelo peixe: vem da comida, e as principais suspeitas são bactérias. Criado longe delas, o baiacu fica sem veneno. Ainda assim, o Japão proíbe servir o fígado.
explicacao: A toxina do baiacu é a tetrodotoxina. Ela bloqueia os canais de sódio dos nervos e paralisa os músculos, enquanto a vítima continua consciente; a morte vem por asfixia. Não existe antídoto conhecido: o tratamento é manter a respiração e a circulação até o corpo eliminar o veneno. Pesquisadores concluíram que o peixe não fabrica a toxina. Ele a acumula ao comer outros animais, e a explicação mais aceita é que ela venha de bactérias, como espécies de Vibrio e Shewanella; com o tempo, o peixe fica insensível a ela. Ainda se discute se a toxina é captada do ambiente ou produzida por bactérias que vivem em simbiose com o peixe. A consequência prática é que criadores conseguem produzir baiacu sem veneno, só mantendo os peixes longe dessas bactérias. No Japão, desde 1958 quem prepara fugu para o público precisa de licença, obtida depois de anos de aprendizado e de uma prova em que só cerca de 35% passam. O fígado, tido como a parte mais saborosa, é também a mais venenosa, e servi-lo em restaurantes é proibido desde 1984. A província de Saga pediu três vezes para liberar o fígado do seu baiacu criado, alegando que ele não é tóxico. A comissão de segurança alimentar recusou todas, por falta de dados que provem a segurança.

fontes.trecho: Restaurant preparation of fugu is strictly controlled by law in Japan, Korea and several other countries [...] The liver, widely thought to be the most flavorful part, was traditionally served as a dish named fugu-kimo, but it is also the most poisonous, and serving this organ in restaurants was banned in Japan in 1984. [...] The poison, a sodium channel blocker, paralyzes the muscles while the victim stays fully conscious; the poisoned victim is unable to breathe and eventually dies from asphyxiation. There is no known antidote for fugu poison. The standard treatment is to support the respiratory and circulatory systems until the poison is metabolized and excreted by the victim's body. Researchers have determined that a fugu's tetrodotoxin comes from eating other animals infested with tetrodotoxin-laden bacteria, to which the fish develops insensitivity over time. Whether tetrodotoxin is sequestered from or produced by symbiotic bacteria is still debated. [...] Farmers now produce poison-free fugu by keeping the fish away from the bacteria [...] TTX is not produced by pufferfish and the other aquatic animals from which it has been isolated. Rather, bacteria such as Alteromonas, Shewanella, and Vibrio species infect or cohabit with the animal species from which TTX is isolated [...] Since 1958, fugu chefs must earn a license to prepare and sell fugu to the public. This involves a two- or three-year apprenticeship. [...] Only about 35 percent of the applicants pass. [...] The Saga Prefecture in Japan has petitioned the Food Safety Commission of Japan three times to reconsider its ban on fugu liver, stating that its farmed fugu is non-toxic. The FSCJ has rejected the proposals thrice due to "data insufficient to prove safety".

gancho: Em Ishikawa, no Japão, o ovário do baiacu, um dos órgãos mais venenosos do peixe, vira iguaria: fica três anos salgado e em conserva de farelo de arroz, e só é vendido depois de passar por testes de toxicidade.
explicacao: No baiacu, a tetrodotoxina se concentra em alguns órgãos, sobretudo fígado, ovários, olhos e pele. Nas estatísticas de intoxicação do Japão, segundo um instituto de pesquisa sobre o fugu, 43% das vítimas tinham comido os ovários, atrás só do fígado, com 50%. Mesmo assim, na cozinha de Hakusan, na província de Ishikawa, esse órgão é servido depois de um processo longo para reduzir o veneno: os ovários são salgados e depois curtidos em pasta de farelo de arroz, num prato chamado "ovários de baiacu em conserva de farelo de arroz". O processo leva três anos. Estima-se que, depois de um ano de conserva, ainda reste cerca de 10% da toxina. O prato só é feito em alguns distritos específicos de Ishikawa, e apenas o método tradicional é permitido. Mesmo depois dos três anos, o produto só vai à venda depois de uma inspeção de toxicidade e de outros testes de segurança, e quem não é do ramo é desaconselhado a tentar o processo por conta própria.

fontes.trecho: Fugu contains lethal amounts of the poison tetrodotoxin in its organs, especially the liver, ovaries, eyes, and skin. [...] According to the Fugu Research Institute, 50% of the victims were poisoned by eating the liver, 43% from eating the ovaries, and 7% from eating the skin. [...] In the cuisine of Hakusan, Ishikawa, ovaries are served after reducing the toxin level by salting and pickling for three years, in a dish named "blowfish ovaries pickled in rice-bran paste" [...] The dish is only made in specific regions of Ishikawa Prefecture (Mikawa district, Ono district, Kanaiwa district, and Wajima), and only the traditional method is permitted. Non-professionals are warned against attempting the process. After one year of pickling, about 10% of the toxin is suggested to remain, and after the full three years the product is "only sold after having been checked for safety through a toxicity inspection, and other tests."

gancho: O akee, fruta nacional da Jamaica, só é colhido depois de se abrir sozinho na árvore. Verde, ele tem uma toxina que derruba o açúcar do sangue. Ao amadurecer, as sementes parecem ajudar a tirar o veneno da polpa.
explicacao: O akee é nativo da África Ocidental e chegou à Jamaica antes de 1773. Lá virou fruta nacional, e o prato nacional oficial é o akee com bacalhau. A parte comida é o arilo, uma polpa cremosa em volta de três sementes pretas. O arilo verde e as partes não comestíveis do fruto contêm hipoglicinas, as "toxinas da saboneteira". No corpo, a hipoglicina A vira um composto que trava a queima de gorduras nas células. Sem esse combustível, o organismo gasta as reservas de glicose e não consegue fabricar mais, e o açúcar do sangue despenca. O quadro, chamado "doença do vômito jamaicana", começa com dor de barriga e vômitos súbitos e, nos casos graves, leva a convulsões, coma e morte. A mortalidade era de 80% até que, em 1954, se passou a infundir glicose nos doentes. A regra tradicional é deixar o fruto se abrir por completo antes de colher: quando ele "bocejou" ou "sorriu", as sementes são descartadas e os arilos são cozidos. Um estudo de 2011 sugeriu uma parte do porquê: durante o amadurecimento, a hipoglicina A do arilo é convertida em hipoglicina B nas sementes, que funcionam como um ralo para a toxina.

fontes.trecho: It is native to tropical West Africa. [...] Ackee is the national fruit of Jamaica and is considered a delicacy. [...] When it ripens it turns from green to a bright red to yellow-orange and splits open to reveal three large, shiny black seeds, each partly surrounded by soft, creamy or spongy, white to yellow flesh [...] Imported to Jamaica from West Africa before 1773, the use of ackee in Jamaican cuisine is prominent. Ackee is the national fruit of Jamaica, while ackee and saltfish is the official national dish of Jamaica. The ackee is allowed to open fully before picking in order to eliminate toxicity. When it has "yawned" or "smiled", the seeds are discarded and the fresh, firm arils are parboiled in salted water or milk [...] The unripened aril and the inedible portions of the fruit contain hypoglycin toxins including hypoglycin A and hypoglycin B, known as "soapberry toxins". [...] Glucose stores are consequently depleted leading to hypoglycemia, and to a condition called Jamaican vomiting sickness. [...] In 2011, it was found that as the fruit ripens, the seeds act as a sink whereby the hypoglycin A in the arils convert to hypoglycin B in the seeds. In other words, the seeds help in detoxifying the arils

Abdominal discomfort begins two to six hours after eating unripe ackee fruit, followed by sudden onset vomiting. In severe cases, profound dehydration, seizures, coma, and death may ensue. [...] When ingested, hypoglycin A is metabolized to produce methylenecyclopropylacetic acid (MCPA). MCPA acts to inhibit the beta-oxidation of fatty acids in two ways. [...] Once the liver glycogen stores are depleted, the body cannot synthesize glucose, and severe hypoglycemia results. [...] mortality was 80% before glucose infusion was introduced in 1954.

gancho: Desde 1995, um surto anual de doença cerebral matava crianças numa região de lichias da Índia, e se suspeitava de infecções e pesticidas. A pista: crianças desnutridas comendo lichias, sobretudo verdes, de barriga vazia.
explicacao: Os surtos aconteciam no distrito de Muzaffarpur, no estado de Bihar, com pico em junho, e diminuíam semanas depois, com as chuvas da monção. A época coincidia com a colheita da lichia, que é forte na região. Muitas causas foram propostas, de encefalites infecciosas a pesticidas. Em 2013 e 2014, o centro indiano de controle de doenças e o CDC americano investigaram e não acharam nenhum agente infeccioso. Viram, sim, que muitas crianças chegavam ao hospital com hipoglicemia, o açúcar do sangue muito baixo. Em 2013, 44% dos casos foram fatais; em 2014, a mortalidade caiu para 31%, e o CDC acha que a recomendação de medir e corrigir a glicose logo na chegada pode ter ajudado. Desde 1962 se sabia que as sementes da lichia têm MCPG, substância aparentada à hipoglicina A do akee jamaicano, fruta da mesma família botânica, que também provoca hipoglicemia. A investigação acabou ligando a doença à hipoglicina A e ao MCPG em crianças desnutridas que comiam lichias, principalmente verdes, sem ter jantado. A recomendação passou a ser limitar a lichia e garantir que as crianças façam a refeição da noite. A explicação não é unânime: um estudo de 2017 em Bangladesh apontou pesticidas das plantações como possíveis responsáveis por casos parecidos.

fontes.titulo: Outbreaks of Unexplained Neurologic Illness — Muzaffarpur, India, 2013–2014 (CDC, MMWR)
fontes.trecho: Outbreaks of an unexplained acute neurologic illness affecting young children and associated with high case-fatality rates have been reported in the Muzaffarpur district of Bihar state in India since 1995. The outbreaks generally peak in June and decline weeks later with the onset of monsoon rains. There have been multiple epidemiologic and laboratory investigations of this syndrome, leading to a wide spectrum of proposed causes for the illness, including infectious encephalitis and exposure to pesticides. An association between illness and litchi fruit has been postulated because Muzaffarpur is a litchi fruit–producing region [...] An ongoing 2014 investigation has found no evidence of any infectious etiology and supports the possibility that exposure to a toxin might be the cause. The outbreak period coincides with the month-long litchi harvesting season in Muzaffarpur. [...] the implementation of the 2013 recommendations for rapid assessment and correction of hypoglycemia might, in part, have helped to reduce mortality (44% in 2013 versus 31% in 2014). [...] MCPG is hypothesized to cause acute hypoglycemia and illness through a similar mechanism to hypoglycin A, a toxin that has been reported to cause acute encephalopathy in the West Indies and West Africa after consumption of unripe ackee, a fruit in the same botanical family as litchi

In 1962 it was found that lychee seeds contain methylenecyclopropylglycine (MCPG), a homologue of hypoglycin A, which causes hypoglycemia in human and animal studies. [...] Because low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) of less than 70 mg/dL in the undernourished children on admission was common, and associated with a poorer outcome (44% of all cases were fatal), the CDC identified the illness as a hypoglycemic encephalopathy. The investigation linked the illness to hypoglycin A and MCPG toxicity and to malnourished children eating lychees (particularly unripe ones) on an empty stomach. The CDC report recommended that parents ensure their children limit lychee consumption and have an evening meal, elevating blood glucose levels that may be sufficient to deter illness. [...] A 2017 study found that pesticides used in the plantations could be responsible for the encephalitis and deaths of young children in Bangladesh.

gancho: Feijão-vermelho cru faz mal: quatro ou cinco grãos já podem dar náusea e vômitos, e panelas elétricas de cozimento lento já foram ligadas a surtos. A proteína culpada virou ferramenta de laboratório.
explicacao: A culpada é a fito-hemaglutinina, uma lectina, proteína que se liga a açúcares e faz as células do sangue se aglutinarem. Ela aparece em vários feijões, mas a maior concentração está no feijão-vermelho: o feijão-branco da mesma espécie tem cerca de um terço, e a fava, de 5% a 10%. A intoxicação começa com náusea intensa e vômitos de uma a três horas depois de comer, e a recuperação costuma ser rápida e espontânea. Só no Reino Unido houve sete surtos entre 1976 e 1979. A proteína é destruída pelo cozimento certo: um estudo mostrou que dez minutos de fervura a 100 °C bastam, e a FDA recomenda ferver por pelo menos 30 minutos para garantir. O problema das panelas de cozimento lento é que a comida dentro delas muitas vezes não passa de 75 °C, o que não destrói a toxina. Feijão em lata é seguro porque já vem cozido. Em 1960, o patologista Peter Nowell, da Universidade da Pensilvânia, usava essa lectina só para ajudar a separar os glóbulos brancos do sangue e descobriu que ela faz os linfócitos se dividirem. Até então se achava que essas células não se dividiam mais. A descoberta teve grande impacto no estudo de doenças cromossômicas.

fontes.titulo: Bad Bug Book, 2nd ed.: Phytohaemagglutinin (kidney bean lectin) (FDA)
fontes.trecho: Among the lectins known to have toxic effects is phytohaemagglutinin, which occurs at relatively high levels in the seeds of legumes (e.g., beans). [...] Toxic dose: As few as four or five raw beans can trigger symptoms. [...] Usually begins with extreme nausea and vomiting within 1 to 3 hours of ingestion of the product [...] Seven outbreaks occurred in the U.K. between 1976 and 1979. [...] White kidney beans, another variety of Phaseolus vulgaris, contain about one-third the amount of toxin as the red variety; broad beans (Vicia faba) contain 5% to 10% the amount that red kidney beans contain. [...] Bender and Readi found that boiling the beans for 10 minutes (100°C) completely destroyed the toxin. Consumers should boil the beans for at least 30 minutes to ensure that the product reaches sufficient temperature, for a sufficient amount of time, to completely destroy the toxin. Slow cookers should not be used to cook these beans or dishes that contain them. Studies of casseroles cooked in slow cookers revealed that the food often reached internal temperatures of only 75°C or less, which is inadequate for destruction of the toxin. [...] Several outbreaks have been associated with beans cooked in slow cookers

Phytohaemagglutinin (PHA, or phytohemagglutinin) is a lectin found in plants, especially certain legumes. [...] These proteins cause blood cells to clump together. [...] Phytohaemagglutinin has carbohydrate-binding specificity for a complex oligosaccharide [...] Recovery is usually spontaneous and rapid, occurring within three to four hours after onset of symptoms [...] Prior to 1960, crude extracts of PHA were known to coat the surface of red blood cells, make them heavier, and thereby improve the separation of the white cell buffy coat. Peter Nowell, an immunologist and pathologist at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, was using PHA for this purpose in 1960 when he discovered it also had the ability to stimulate mitotic division of lymphocytes from normal peripheral blood. Prior to his discovery, these cells were assumed to be the terminal end-products of differentiation. This work had tremendous implications for the constitutional study of chromosomal disorders.
Canned red kidney beans, though, are safe to eat straight from the can, as they are cooked prior to being shipped.

gancho: O verde da batata é clorofila e, sozinho, não faz mal. Mas é um alarme: a luz que o produz também faz a batata fabricar solanina, uma defesa tóxica. E ferver a batata quase não destrói essa toxina.
explicacao: A batata é parente da beladona e do tabaco, e a planta inteira produz glicoalcaloides, principalmente solanina e chaconina, que funcionam como pesticida natural contra insetos, doenças e herbívoros. Folhas, caules e brotos têm muito; o tubérculo bem guardado tem pouco. Quando fica exposto à luz, porém, ele esverdeia e aumenta a produção dessas defesas, para não ser comido. Ferimentos, brotação e armazenamento longo também elevam os níveis, e 30% a 80% da solanina fica na casca ou perto dela. O cozimento ajuda pouco: a fervura reduz a alfa-solanina em só 1,2% e a alfa-chaconina em 3,5%, porque esses compostos só começam a se decompor por volta de 170 °C. Intoxicações graves são raras, mas acontecem: no fim da década de 1970, 78 alunos de uma escola no Reino Unido passaram mal depois de comer batatas mal armazenadas durante o verão, e dezessete foram hospitalizados, todos recuperados. O problema também pode vir do melhoramento genético: a variedade Lenape, lançada em 1967, foi retirada em 1970 por ter glicoalcaloides demais. Desde então, os melhoristas testam esse teor e às vezes descartam variedades promissoras por causa dele.

fontes.trecho: Solanine has pesticidal properties, and it is one of the plant's natural defenses. [...] For example, boiling potatoes reduces the α-chaconine and α-solanine levels by only 3.5% and 1.2% respectively [...] Alkaloids like solanine have been shown to start decomposing and degrading at approximately 170 °C (338 °F) [...] There was a mass solanine poisoning incident in 1979 in the U.K., when 78 adolescent boys at a boarding school exhibited symptoms after eating potatoes that had been stored improperly over the summer. Seventeen of them ended up hospitalized, but they all recovered. [...] Potatoes naturally produce solanine and chaconine, a related glycoalkaloid, as a defense mechanism against insects, disease, and herbivores. Potato leaves, stems, and shoots are naturally high in glycoalkaloids. When potato tubers are exposed to light, they turn green and increase glycoalkaloid production. This is a natural defense to help prevent the uncovered tuber from being eaten. The green colour is from chlorophyll, and is itself harmless. However, it is an indication that increased level of solanine and chaconine may be present. In potato tubers, 30–80% of the solanine develops in and close to the skin [...] Though fatalities from solanine poisoning are rare, there have been several notable cases of human solanine poisonings.

Raw potatoes contain toxic glycoalkaloids, of which the most prevalent are solanine and chaconine. Solanine is found in other plants in the same family, Solanaceae, which includes such plants as deadly nightshade (Atropa belladonna), henbane (Hyoscyamus niger) and tobacco [...] Exposure to light, physical damage, and age increase glycoalkaloid content within the tuber. [...] The 'Lenape' variety, released in 1967, was withdrawn in 1970 as it contained high levels of glycoalkaloids. Since then, breeders of new varieties test for this, sometimes discarding an otherwise promising cultivar.

gancho: Na Primeira Guerra Mundial, as folhas do ruibarbo, que são tóxicas, foram recomendadas por engano como alimento na Grã-Bretanha, e houve intoxicações. Da planta, só o talo é comestível.
explicacao: Do ruibarbo se come o talo, a haste que segura a folha, em geral cozido com açúcar em tortas e doces. Esse uso é recente: foi registrado pela primeira vez na Inglaterra dos séculos XVIII e XIX, quando o açúcar ficou mais barato. As folhas grandes e triangulares são outra história. Elas têm muito ácido oxálico, que agride os rins, além de outros compostos tóxicos, e por isso não são comestíveis. Mesmo assim, durante a Primeira Guerra elas foram recomendadas como alimento na Grã-Bretanha, e pessoas se intoxicaram. Há um detalhe que contraria a fama da planta: comer um pouco de folha não costuma causar sintomas graves. Os casos graves, aliás, são mal documentados e parecem ter vindo do consumo em grande quantidade e por muito tempo, como numa dieta de guerra. O ácido oxálico também pode migrar das folhas para os talos quando a planta sofre geada forte, e por isso não se recomenda comer ruibarbo danificado pelo frio. Thomas Jefferson plantou uma espécie de ruibarbo em Monticello em 1809 e anotou que as folhas eram "excelentes como espinafre".

fontes.trecho: The large, triangular leaves contain high levels of oxalic acid and anthrone glycosides, making them poisonous and therefore inedible. [...] The species Rheum rhabarbarum (syn. R. undulatum) [...] Rhubarb damaged by severe cold should not be eaten, as it may be high in oxalic acid, which migrates from the leaves and can cause illness. [...] Thomas Jefferson planted R. undulatum at Monticello in 1809 and 1811, observing that it was "Esculent rhubarb, the leaves excellent as Spinach." [...] Rhubarb is grown primarily for its sour, fleshy leafstalks, technically known as petioles. The use of rhubarb stalks as food is a relatively recent innovation. This usage was first recorded in 18th- to 19th-century England after affordable sugar became more widely available. Commonly, it is stewed with sugar or used in pies and desserts [...] Rhubarb leaves contain poisonous substances, including oxalic acid, a nephrotoxin. [...] Humans have been poisoned after ingesting the leaves, a particular problem during World War I when the leaves were mistakenly recommended as a food source in Britain. The printed information recommending the leaves as a food source was rediscovered during World War 2 and redistributed, leading to further deaths. This phenomenon occurred due to long term and high quantity exposure to rhubarb leaves. Contrary to popular belief, rhubarb leaves do not cause severe symptoms or death in low amounts. [...] Serious cases of rhubarb poisoning are not well documented.

gancho: A castanha-de-caju não é vendida com casca por um motivo: a casca tem um óleo que irrita a pele, quimicamente parente do da hera venenosa. Caju, manga e pistache são da mesma família de plantas.
explicacao: O caju é nativo da América do Sul tropical, e os portugueses o espalharam pela Índia e outras regiões tropicais no século XVI. O que chamamos de fruta é um pedúnculo inchado; o fruto verdadeiro é a castanha pendurada na ponta, uma semente envolta numa casca dupla. Essa casca contém ácido anacárdico, um irritante potente da pele, quimicamente aparentado ao urushiol, o óleo alergênico da hera venenosa e da árvore da laca. Por isso a castanha crua e a casca são tóxicas, e ela só vira petisco depois de descascada e torrada ou cozida no vapor. O contato com esse óleo é um risco para quem processa caju à mão. O líquido da casca, porém, é aproveitado como matéria-prima de resinas, tintas, vernizes e materiais de atrito. O parentesco químico tem uma razão botânica: o caju dá nome à família das anacardiáceas, que inclui a manga, o pistache e a árvore da laca, e cujos membros às vezes produzem urushiol. A manga também pode causar dermatite: o contato com a seiva, as folhas e a casca da fruta é a causa mais comum de dermatite por plantas no Havaí durante a safra, e quem já reagiu ao urushiol pode correr mais risco.

fontes.trecho: Cashews are native to tropical South America. Portuguese explorers encountered them in the 16th century and spread them to India and other tropical regions of the world. [...] The nut shell and raw seed are toxic, but the nut is edible once shelled and roasted or steamed. [...] The drupe first develops on the tree and then the pedicel expands to become the cashew apple. The drupe becomes the true fruit, a single shell-encased seed, which is often considered a nut in the culinary sense. The seed is surrounded by a double-shell that contains an allergenic phenolic resin, anacardic acid - which is a potent skin irritant chemically related to the better-known and also toxic allergenic oil urushiol, which is found in the related poison ivy and lacquer tree. [...] Because it can cause dermatitis, cashews are typically not sold in the shell to consumers. [...] Anacardic acid is also used in the chemical industry for the production of cardanol, which is used for resins, coatings, and frictional materials. These substances are skin allergens, like lacquer and the oils of poison ivy, and they present a danger during manual cashew processing. [...] Derivatives of the shell are also used in paints.

The Anacardiaceae, commonly known as the cashew family or sumac family, are a family of flowering plants [...] Members of the Anacardiaceae bear fruits that are drupes and in some cases produce urushiol, an irritant. The Anacardiaceae include numerous genera, several of which are economically important, notably cashew (in the type genus Anacardium), mango, Chinese lacquer tree [...] The genus Pistacia (which includes the pistachio and mastic tree) is now included

Contact with oils in mango leaves, stems, sap, and skin can cause dermatitis and anaphylaxis in susceptible individuals. Those with a history of contact dermatitis induced by urushiol (an allergen found in poison ivy, poison oak, or poison sumac) may be most at risk for mango contact dermatitis. [...] During the primary ripening season of mangoes, contact with mango plant parts – primarily sap, leaves, and fruit skin – is the most common cause of plant dermatitis in Hawaii.

gancho: No fim do século V a.C., soldados gregos comeram favos perto do mar Negro e caíram como se tivessem perdido uma batalha. Era o "mel louco", feito do néctar de rododendros, produzido até hoje na Turquia e no Nepal.
explicacao: O relato é de Xenofonte, no livro Anábase. Perto da atual Trabzon, os soldados que comeram os favos perderam os sentidos, vomitaram, tiveram diarreia e não conseguiam ficar de pé. No dia seguinte, ninguém tinha morrido, e eles se recuperaram mais ou menos na mesma hora em que tinham passado mal. O culpado são as graianotoxinas, presentes no néctar de rododendros e de outras plantas da família das ericáceas. Elas afetam os nervos e o coração e podem derrubar a pressão e os batimentos, mas, com tratamento, a intoxicação raramente mata. O mel também apareceu na guerra: em 65 a.C., o rei Mitrídates deixou favos pelo caminho das tropas romanas de Pompeu, e os soldados intoxicados foram mortos. Em 1891, um cientista alemão isolou a toxina do mel de Trabzon. Mesmo assim, a Enciclopédia Britânica de 1929 descartou os relatos antigos, dizendo que os sintomas provavelmente vinham de comer demais. Hoje o mel louco, chamado deli bal na Turquia, é usado como medicina tradicional e droga recreativa. Segundo a FDA, méis importados da Turquia já causaram intoxicações em outros países. O mel industrial costuma ser seguro porque mistura méis de muitas origens, o que dilui qualquer toxina.

fontes.trecho: Mad honey is honey that contains grayanotoxins. The dark, reddish honey is produced from the nectar and pollen of genus Rhododendron and has both toxic and narcotic effects. Mad honey is produced principally in Nepal and Turkey, where it is used both as a traditional medicine and a recreational drug. [...] The Greek military leader and historian Xenophon wrote an account of a 401 BCE incident involving mad honey in his work Anabasis about the expedition of the Ten Thousand. In his account, he describes how Greek soldiers traveling near Trabzon (now part of Turkey) near the Black Sea, ate mad honey and then became disoriented, suffering vomiting and diarrhea, and no longer able to stand. [...] They lay upon the ground, in consequence, in great numbers, as if there had been a defeat; and there was general dejection. The next day no one of them was found dead; and they recovered their senses about the same hour that they had lost them on the preceding day [...] In 65 BCE, during the Third Mithridatic War, King Mithridates staged a strategic withdrawal from Roman soldiers under General Pompey. [...] Mithridates had the withdrawing soldiers place combs of mad honey on their path. The Roman soldiers who ate the honey succumbed to mad honey intoxication and were slain. [...] The chemical compound andromedotoxin (grayanotoxin I) was isolated from Trabzon honey by German scientist P. C. Plugge in 1891. The 1929 edition of the Encyclopædia Britannica dismissed the notion of poison honey as described in Greek and Roman texts, concluding that "in all likelihood the symptoms described by these old writers were due to overeating" [...] In contrast, large-scale honey production often mixes honey gathered from different locations, diluting the concentration of any contaminated honey. [...] In Turkey, mad honey is known as deli bal and is used as a recreational drug and traditional medicine.

Grayanotoxin is found in the leaves, flowers, and nectar of some Rhododendron species and from other members of the Ericaceæ botanical family. [...] In other countries, however, some honeys imported from Turkey have recently caused mad honey sickness. [...] The toxin affects nerve cells, including not only the nerves that affect the brain, but also those that affect the heart and other muscles. [...] but also irregular or very slow heartbeat, low blood pressure, and fainting. These poisonings are rarely fatal.

gancho: Mais de 400 milhões de pessoas têm deficiência de G6PD, uma enzima dos glóbulos vermelhos. Nelas, a fava pode destruir essas células. A mutação parece ter se espalhado por dar proteção contra a malária.
explicacao: A G6PD ajuda os glóbulos vermelhos a se defender de compostos oxidantes. Quem tem a deficiência, a mais comum do mundo entre as que causam anemia por defeito de enzima, quase sempre não sente nada. Os problemas surgem com gatilhos: infecções, certos remédios e alimentos, sobretudo a fava, que dá nome ao favismo. A fava contém substâncias como a vicina e a convicina, que geram oxidantes; sem a enzima, as defesas da célula se esgotam e os glóbulos vermelhos se rompem. Nem todos os portadores reagem à fava, e as crianças são as mais afetadas. O favismo é mais comum na bacia do Mediterrâneo, e a Sardenha tem a maior frequência de favismo registrada, cinco casos por mil pessoas. O motivo provável é a malária. Há duas explicações propostas: o parasita é muito sensível a danos oxidativos, e as células infectadas podem ser eliminadas mais depressa pelo baço, o que daria vantagem aos portadores em regiões com a doença. A história moderna do problema também passa pela malária. Durante a Guerra da Coreia, os militares americanos deram em massa o antimalárico primaquina, e muitos soldados tiveram anemia por destruição dos glóbulos vermelhos. Estudos mostraram depois que o defeito estava nas próprias células.

fontes.trecho: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (G6PDD), also known as favism, is the most common enzyme deficiency anemia worldwide. [...] Most of the time, those who are affected have no symptoms. [...] Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase is an enzyme that protects red blood cells, which carry oxygen from the lungs to tissues throughout the body, from reactive oxygen species. [...] Red blood cell breakdown may be triggered by infections, certain medication, stress, or foods such as fava beans. [...] Favism is a hemolytic response to the consumption of fava beans, also known as broad beans. Though all individuals with favism show G6PD deficiency, not all individuals with G6PD deficiency show favism. The condition is more prevalent in infants and children [...] Broad beans, e.g., fava beans, contain high levels of vicine, divicine, convicine, and isouramil, all of which create oxidants. When all remaining reduced glutathione is consumed, enzymes and other proteins (including hemoglobin) are subsequently damaged by the oxidants [...] G6PD deficiency is the second most common human enzyme defect after ALDH2 deficiency, being present in more than 400 million people worldwide. [...] The Mediterranean Basin is where favism is most common [...] Sardinia has the highest reported frequency of favism, with five instances per 1,000 people. A side effect of this disease is that it confers protection against malaria, in particular the form of malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum, the most deadly form of malaria. [...] One theory to explain this is that cells infected with the Plasmodium parasite are cleared more rapidly by the spleen. This phenomenon might give G6PD deficiency carriers an evolutionary advantage by increasing their fitness in malaria-endemic environments. In vitro studies have shown that Plasmodium falciparum is very sensitive to oxidative damage. [...] Despite these results, the US military administered the drug widely during the Korean War to prevent the relapsing infection caused by Plasmodium vivax hypnozoites. Numerous cases of hemolytic anemia were observed in US soldiers of North African and Mediterranean descent. After studying the mechanism through Cr51 testing, it was conclusively shown that the hemolytic effect of primaquine was due to an intrinsic defect of erythrocytes.

gancho: Os inuítes não comem fígado de urso-polar: ele tem vitamina A em excesso. Exploradores europeus aprenderam isso passando mal em 1597. Esse excesso é a suspeita principal da morte de um explorador na Antártida, em 1913.
explicacao: A vitamina A pronta, a de origem animal, é absorvida com muita eficiência e se acumula no fígado. Em excesso, ela é tóxica. O fígado de alguns animais do Ártico, como o urso-polar, a foca-barbuda e a morsa, é especialmente perigoso, e os inuítes há muito tempo evitam o de urso-polar e o de foca-barbuda. Alguns predadores do Ártico, como o urso-polar e a foca-barbuda, chegam a ter de 10 a 20 vezes mais vitamina A no fígado que animais de fora do Ártico, mas mantêm o nível no sangue sob controle. Entre europeus, o primeiro registro conhecido é de 1597: Gerrit de Veer contou no diário que ele e seus homens, abrigados no inverno em Nova Zembla, adoeceram depois de comer fígado de urso-polar. Na Antártida, o suíço Xavier Mertz e Douglas Mawson perderam o companheiro Belgrave Ninnis e um trenó com a maior parte da comida numa fenda no gelo. Na volta, comeram os cães, inclusive o fígado. Mertz morreu no caminho, em janeiro de 1913. Um estudo de 1969 concluiu que os sintomas descritos por Mawson, como perda de cabelo e de pele, indicavam excesso de vitamina A, a explicação mais aceita até hoje, embora frio e desnutrição também sejam apontados. Já o betacaroteno das frutas e verduras não causa esse problema: no máximo deixa a pele alaranjada.

fontes.trecho: Hypervitaminosis A refers to the toxic effects of ingesting too much preformed vitamin A [...] Overconsumption of beta-carotene can only cause carotenosis, a harmless and reversible cosmetic condition in which the skin turns orange. Preformed vitamin A absorption and storage in the liver occur very efficiently until a pathologic condition develops. [...] The liver of certain animals, including the polar bear, bearded seal, and walrus, is particularly toxic [...] Vitamin A toxicity has long been known to the Inuit, as they will not eat the liver of polar bears or bearded seals due to them containing dangerous amounts of Vitamin A. It has been known to Europeans since at least 1597 when Gerrit de Veer wrote in his diary that, while taking refuge in the winter in Nova Zemlya, he and his men became severely ill after eating polar bear liver. [...] Some Arctic animals demonstrate no signs of hypervitaminosis A despite having 10–20 times the level of vitamin A in their livers as non-Arctic animals. These animals are top predators and include the polar bear, Arctic fox, bearded seal, and glaucous gull. Plasma concentrations are maintained in a non-toxic range despite the high liver content.

Dr Xavier Guillaume Mertz (6 October 1882 – 8 January 1913) was a Swiss polar explorer [...] In early 1911, Mertz was hired by geologist and explorer Douglas Mawson for his Antarctic expedition. [...] After Ninnis and a sledge carrying most of the food disappeared down a crevasse, 311 miles (500 km) from the expedition's main hut, Mertz and Mawson headed back west, gradually using the dogs to supplement their remaining food stocks. About 100 miles (160 km) from safety, Mertz died, leaving Mawson to carry on alone. The cause of Mertz's death has never been firmly established; the commonly purported theory is hypervitaminosis A [...] Other theories suggest he may have died from a combination of malnutrition, cold exposure, and psychological stresses. [...] they ate all parts of the animals, including their livers. [...] A 1969 study by Sir John Cleland and Ronald Vernon Southcott, of the University of Adelaide, concluded that the symptoms Mawson described—hair, skin and weight loss, depression, dysentery, and persistent skin infections—indicated the men had suffered hypervitaminosis A, an excessive intake of vitamin A. [...] This theory is the most widely accepted, but there have been other theories.

gancho: O chícharo, uma leguminosa, dá colheita quando as outras falham. Mas, se vira a base da dieta por meses, pode paralisar as pernas para sempre. Goya gravou essa tragédia na Espanha de Napoleão.
explicacao: O chícharo, Lathyrus sativus, é uma leguminosa plantada na Ásia e no leste da África, importante em regiões sujeitas a seca e fome. Suas sementes contêm ODAP, uma neurotoxina que superexcita receptores de neurônios na medula espinhal e no córtex. Quando o grão vira a principal fonte de proteína por um período longo, o resultado pode ser o neurolatirismo: os neurônios motores das pernas morrem, e a fraqueza progride até a pessoa não conseguir andar. A paralisia é irreversível, mas não encurta a vida. O paradoxo é cruel: a planta acumula mais toxina justamente sob seca e outros estresses, quando é mais necessária. Na fome da Etiópia de 1984 e 1985, foram registrados 2.542 casos só na região de Wollo. Durante a guerra de independência espanhola contra Napoleão, o chícharo serviu de comida de fome, e Goya o retratou na gravura "Gracias a la almorta" ("Graças ao chícharo"), com uma mulher que já não consegue andar entre pessoas famintas à espera de uma tigela. A Espanha proibiu vender produtos de chícharo para consumo humano de 1967 a 2018. Deixar de molho, ferver, fermentar, descascar e germinar o grão reduzem a toxina, e há programas de melhoramento para criar variedades com pouco ODAP.

fontes.trecho: is a legume (family Fabaceae) commonly grown for human consumption and livestock feed in Asia and East Africa. It is a particularly important crop in areas that are prone to drought and famine, and is thought of as an 'insurance crop' as it produces reliable yields when all other crops fail. The seeds contain a neurotoxin that causes lathyrism, a neurodegenerative disease, if eaten as a primary protein source for a prolonged period. [...] Neurolathyrism or lathyrism is a chronic, progressive and irreversible neurodegenerative disease affecting motor neurons of the lower limbs . The disease is characterized by progressive spastic weakness of the lower limbs, which may eventually lead to the inability to walk . However, it has no impact on longevity or cognitive functions. [...] One of the largest documented outbreaks occurred during the 1984–1985 Ethiopian famine in the Wollo region, where 2,542 cases of lathyrism were recorded following increased reliance on grass pea consumption. [...] It depicts a woman who can no longer walk due to lathyrism, surrounded by starving people waiting for bowls of grass pea-based food. Grass-pea products were banned for sale for human consumption in Spain from 1967 to 2018, due to toxicity. [...] After the ODAP crosses the blood-brain barrier, it binds to AMPA-receptors in the spinal cord and cortex and activates them. This activation leads to an excessive calcium influx, which overstimulates neuronal pathways [...] ODAP synthesis is associated with plant nitrogen and sulfur metabolism and has been reported to increase under environmental stress conditions, including drought, salinity, nutrient deficiency, and sulfur limitation . [...] Soaking, boiling, fermentation, dehulling, and germination have been shown to lower ODAP concentrations in seeds . [...] Breeding programs are underway to produce lines of Lathyrus sativus that contain ODAP levels too low to be dangerous

During the Spanish War of Independence against Napoleon, grasspea served as a famine food. This was the subject of one of Francisco de Goya's famous aquatint prints titled Gracias a la Almorta ("Thanks to the Grasspea"), depicting poor people surviving on a porridge made from grasspea flour, one of them lying on the floor, already crippled by it.

gancho: Na Idade Média, um fungo do centeio causava o "fogo de Santo Antônio", que gangrenava dedos das mãos e dos pés. A ideia de que ele explica as "enfeitiçadas" de Salem é popular, mas foi rebatida por historiadores.
explicacao: O fungo Claviceps purpurea infecta o centeio e outros cereais e forma grãos escuros, cheios de alcaloides. Comidos com o pão por muito tempo, eles estreitam os vasos sanguíneos e levam à gangrena seca das extremidades; outra forma da doença causa convulsões e alucinações. O apelido vem dos monges da Ordem de Santo Antônio, que se dedicavam a tratar os doentes. Há pelo menos 83 surtos documentados, sobretudo na Europa. Em 1778, uma epidemia na região francesa de Sologne matou mais de 8 mil pessoas, e o médico Tessier recomendou drenar os campos, limpar os grãos e trocar o centeio infectado por batata. Uma prevenção simples é pôr a colheita em salmoura: os grãos do fungo boiam e os sadios afundam. Em 1976, um artigo na revista Science propôs que o fungo explicaria as acusações de bruxaria de Salem, em 1692. Menos de um ano depois, os pesquisadores Nicholas Spanos e Jack Gottlieb rebateram a tese na mesma revista: num surto, famílias inteiras adoeceriam, sobretudo as crianças, o que não aconteceu; vários sintomas típicos não aparecem nos registros; e os surtos convulsivos ocorrem em populações com falta de vitamina A, o que não era o caso de uma comunidade rural com leite à vontade. Historiadores do século XXI mantêm essa conclusão, embora ainda haja quem defenda versões da hipótese.

fontes.trecho: Ergotism (pronounced  UR-gət-iz-əm) is the effect of long-term ergot poisoning, frequently due to the ingestion of the alkaloids produced by the Claviceps purpurea fungus [...] that infects rye and other cereals [...] Ergot alkaloids, the active compounds produced by the ergot fungus, can cause severe vasoconstriction, leading to symptoms like gangrene and convulsions. Additionally, ergot alkaloids can mimic neurotransmitters and hormones in the human body, causing hallucinations [...] It affects the more poorly vascularized distal structures, such as the fingers and toes. [...] Dark-purple or black grain kernels, known as ergot bodies, can be identifiable in the heads of cereal or grass just before harvest. [...] Removal of ergot bodies is done by placing the yield in a brine solution; the ergot bodies float, while the healthy grains sink. [...] Throughout history, at least 83 outbreaks of ergotism have been documented, particularly in Europe. [...] Another possible case is associated with the Salem witch trials in 1692 [...] In the Middle Ages the gangrenous poisoning was known as "holy fire" or "Saint Anthony's fire", named after monks of the Order of St. Anthony, who dedicated themselves to treating this ailment. [...] The French physician Tessier observed a huge epidemic in the year 1778 in Sologne (France), during which more than 8000 people died, and was hence persuaded to recommend drainage of fields, compulsory cleaning of grain and replacement of infected grain with potatoes. [...] This medical explanation for the theory of "bewitchment" was first propounded by Linnda R. Caporael in 1976 in an article in Science. [...] Within a year of Caporael's article, historians Nicholas Spanos and Jack Gottlieb refuted the idea in the same journal. [...] They noted that if ergotism was present in Salem, the symptoms would have occurred by household, not individual. Whole families, and particularly all the young children in a household, would have shown symptoms, but this was not the case. [...] Spanos and Gottlieb also state that most of ergot poisoning's symptoms, like crawling and tingling sensations, vertigo, tinnitus, vomiting, and diarrhea, do not appear in the records of events in Salem. Lastly, they note that convulsive ergotism epidemics only take place in communities suffering from vitamin A deficiencies; they argued that residents of Salem, living in a farming community with ample access to dairy, would have had no reason to be deficient in vitamin A. [...] Historians published in the early 21st century continue to stand by Spanos and Gottlieb's conclusion. Historian Leon Harrier has argued that only some members of a household might have shown symptoms because they had underlying conditions.

gancho: Em Guam, uma doença parecida com ELA, Parkinson e Alzheimer já foi a maior causa de morte de adultos do povo chamorro. Uma hipótese ainda debatida culpa morcegos que comiam sementes tóxicas e eram iguaria local.
explicacao: A doença, chamada lytico-bodig pelos chamorros, foi a principal causa de morte de adultos entre 1945 e 1956 e chegou a ser 100 vezes mais frequente ali do que no resto do mundo. Além da genética, uma das suspeitas é a dieta. Os chamorros fazem farinha das sementes de uma cicadácea local, muito tóxicas ao natural, e por isso deixam a farinha de molho e a lavam várias vezes. Nos anos 1950 se achou nelas a cicasina, uma toxina potente, mas que não reproduzia a doença. Em 1967, inspirados nos estudos que ligaram o chícharo a uma paralisia, pesquisadores acharam outra substância, o BMAA. A quantidade livre na farinha parecia baixa demais, e a pista foi abandonada pela segunda vez. Depois, Paul Alan Cox e Oliver Sacks reabriram o caso. O BMAA é produzido por cianobactérias que vivem nas raízes da cicadácea. Morcegos frugívoros comem as sementes e concentram a substância no corpo, e esses morcegos eram uma iguaria dos chamorros. A queda no consumo dos morcegos acompanhou a queda da doença. Um estudo de 2016 com macacos alimentados com BMAA deu apoio à ideia. Mas a causa continua incerta: a doença corre em famílias, e parte dos pacientes tem mutações em genes conhecidos de doenças neurodegenerativas.

fontes.trecho: is a rare, terminal neurodegenerative disease of uncertain etiology endemic to the Chamorro people of the island of Guam in Micronesia. [...] reflects its resemblance to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), Parkinson's disease, and Alzheimer's disease. [...] The frequency of cases grew amongst the Chamorro until it was the leading cause of adult death between 1945 and 1956. The incidence rate was 200 per 100,000 per year and it was 100 times more prevalent than in the rest of the world. [...] Decline in consumption of the bats has been linked to a decline in the incidence of the disease. [...] Some hypotheses as to the cause of the disease include genetics, cycad seeds, and ingested beta-Methylamino-L-alanine (BMAA) from the consumption of fruit bats. [...] The disease was shown to be familial but not genetic. [...] Targeted high-throughput sequencing in a relatively small sample demonstrates that disease in many patients can be explained by pathogenic mutations in known genes for neurodegeneration. [...] The starch from indigenous Cycas micronesica seeds is consumed in the traditional Chamorro diet. The seeds are ground to make a flour called fadang, and the flour is then used to make flatbread and dumplings. The flour is soaked and washed several times, as the seed in its natural form is extremely toxic. Ample research on the cycad hypothesis found a component of the seeds, cycasin, was a potent toxin; it was discovered in the 1950s. As toxic as it was, it was incapable of causing of the symptoms of lytico-bodig. [...] and the hypothesis was rejected for the first time. In 1967, following studies that linked lathyrism to ODAP, Marjorie Whiting, a nutritional anthropologist, asked Arthur Bell, a plant biochemist, to test cycad seeds for their chemical constituents. Bell and his colleagues discovered another toxic substance in the seeds, BMAA (beta-Methylamino-L-alanine). Initial laboratory results found low levels of free BMAA in cycad flour. The cycad hypothesis was abandoned a second time [...] The cycad hypothesis was resurrected by Paul Alan Cox and Oliver Sacks, after re-examining aspects of the Chamorro diet. Cox and his colleagues found that BMAA is produced by symbiotic cyanobacteria found in the coralloid roots of cycads. Other than that, fruit bats or flying foxes feed on cycad seeds, and were a common food for the Chamorros. The bats bioaccumulate BMAA in their fat [...] Cox also observed decline in fruit bat consumption matching the decline in lytico-bodig. Support for the BMAA theory of the Guam disease came from the finding reported in 2016 that chronic dietary exposure of vervet monkeys

Cycas micronesica seeds, containing β-Methylamino-L-alanine, were made into flour by the Chamorro people of Guam as a dietary staple. [...] Flying foxes, a Chamorro delicacy, forage on the fleshy seed covering of cycad seeds and concentrate the toxin in their bodies.
